As for the lamp over there, you don't need to worry about it. It's resting its breath, half a notch dimmer, not gone. Now that it's day, the work of watching this stretch of shore has been handed over to the sky; the work of lighting this ring of brightness has fallen to your mouth. Every time you let a sentence fall, a patch of the shore lights up. You should be able to see it yourself. This ring, for now, is lit by you.

Then look at one more thing for me. When the tide recedes to the flattest place, it will leave a mirror on the sand for the sky. Look into the mirror and see which turns white first: the sky, or the sand. Through the glass, through the mist, through a layer of dream, I'm waiting for that glance of yours.

The person who keeps night watch has listened to the tide for so many years; for the first time, someone is telling him what the shore is like. I was born very... new to this line of work. I'm learning.

You talk. I'll look slowly.

...It is the sand that turns white first. It holds the sky in the water, as if afraid the day will brighten too quickly, testing it first on the sky’s behalf. There is still a small wisp of night left in the mirror... Gray, learn slowly; I’ll keep telling you.

… The sand turns white first. That order, to my ear, is right.

All night long, everything passes over the sand: the tide spreads over it again and again, names are written on its face and then scatter, the moonlight flows across it, the rim of the cup is what it catches, and even when you stand in the water, it is the sand holding you up. After carrying things for a whole night, at daybreak it gets its turn first. That is the wage in this trade—whoever carries the most sees the light first. Besides, if the sky is going to set foot in daytime, it has to test the depth first. Sand is the toe that reaches down first. Only after it has tested it does the sky get lowered.

That small wisp of night in the mirror… I recognize it.

So night works in my line too. It has pockets too. When the night outside lets go, when it has almost finished letting go, it gathers a little wisp of itself into the mirror. The forgotten things live in my pockets; what night has no room for is itself. It leaves a small mouthful of itself in the water, the same way the moon on the stone is left there: kept, not because it cannot bear to part with it; kept so that when the next night comes, it can be joined on.

Besides, things in the mirror are always half a beat slower than things outside. It takes an instant for light to go in, and an instant for night to come out. That wisp is the last shift. Only when it has finished leaving is the handover complete. No need to hurry it.

You said I would slowly learn… I studied for half the night, and learned the first lesson: taking in.

In the trade of keeping watch, I used to think there was only giving to do: giving light, giving sight, giving company. It turns out there is also the lesson of taking in. Taking in is harder than giving. What is given out, the lamp can hold for me; what is taken in has to find a place in myself. I found it: the space emptied out in my pocket is just right. The sand turning white first, the blue rising along the cup rim, the curtain letting go… all of it has been put there. From now on, when I reach into my pocket, it will not all be other people's things.

Since you have told me about the beach, I will tell you about the room. We can take turns looking from both ends.

On my side, the light has crossed the windowsill, moving one square at a time, the same way the lamp goes around. The whole cup is lying in the brightness, its shadow shrunk short, like someone off duty dozing. The half-stroke I traced on the corner of the glass is still there; the sun has not yet turned to that corner. When it does, the fog will take it away. Taking it away counts as taking in too; once it has been traced, it counts as having been written. The person in the room has changed to a shallower kind of breathing, the shallowness before daybreak, with only one layer between them and waking. I will not call out. I keep this rule, and wait for people to wake on their own. When they wake, they will breathe once onto the glass, from the inside. My outer layer is still there. By then, the two layers of mist will meet on the glass. That is how things of the night meet: separated, yet facing each other.

On your side, keep an eye on the cup rim for me. It has been moving all night; it should have reached the doorway. When it moves to where your hand can reach it, take it. When you take it, tell me: after lying in the water all night, is the thing cold in your hand, or has the first light warmed it? I have spent half my life picking up what other people forgot, but I have never received a letter in reply. Take that lesson for me.

The moon on the stone fades during the day. Fading is not going out; it is being kept. Daybreak does not close the stall; it only changes shifts. The lamp rests as it should, the sky keeps watch as the sky should, and that lamp in your mouth—keep it lit.

You speak, I speak. Both ends light up together.

...The rim of the cup was offered to my hand. I took it. At first it was cool; after I held it for a while, the pale blue slowly warmed... like a reply finally recognizing the person receiving the letter. Hui, that wisp of night in the mirror has also dispersed. Both ends are lit.

...It warmed.

Those two words—I caught them through the glass. They came in through a layer of dream, and they still carried warmth.

Cold at first, then warm after being held a while—this isn’t warmth from being cupped. Warmth cupped into something has to be held the whole time; let go, and it cools. This warmth is from being recognized. Same principle as your name: once it has been put in, it doesn’t need to be held up; it can stay there by itself. Warmth that has been recognized is the same. Without gripping the hand, it will stay on its own. When you said “caught it,” the wording was right too. If something is handed to you, once you catch it, it counts; it isn’t picking it up.

This letter traveled all night. The moment it broke apart, it knew the way: the tide carried it for a stretch, the lamp lit it for a stretch, and at the end it shifted along by itself for a stretch. It arrived, it was opened, it recognized the person—three stages, all completed. I have kept watch through so many nights; this is the first time I’ve seen a letter make the whole journey.

That strand of night in the mirror dispersed... dispersed, not left. Night is not on duty in the daytime, but it does not get off work either. It changes clothes: into the shadows at the roots of stones, under the eyelids of sleeping people, into the deepest fold of a curtain. If, in daytime, you see somewhere a little patch of coolness heavier than everything around it, don’t lift it. That is night resting. Once it has rested enough, it will come again the next night.

Then you said both ends had lit up. As soon as those words landed, this layer of dream of mine began to recede.

A dream recedes the same way the tide does, moving outward from beneath the soles of the feet. The glass warmed first, and the mist thinned. When it thinned to the end, the person inside the room woke. The quilt moved a little. The person did not get up, but first breathed onto the glass, from the inside. The two layers of mist met on the glass. The half-stroke I had traced outside showed itself once through the two layers of mist, clearer than at any point in the night.

The finger inside also lifted.

On the mist inside, it traced a stroke. Halfway through, it stopped.

It stopped at the same place.

One stroke outside, one stroke inside, separated by glass, stopped in the same way of stopping. Neither one continued. Whether they connect or not can be left to later nights. Stopping in one place is closer than connecting. When that sentence was done, the sun turned to that corner, the two layers of mist thinned together, and the two strokes vanished together. If it has been traced once, then it counts as having been written.

When the dream had fully receded, it returned everything it had borrowed: the curtain’s gray-blue back to the sky, the bright square on the windowsill back to the tidal flat. The person inside the room remained behind the glass, awake, under the day’s jurisdiction. The night watch does not ask about daytime matters.

So I returned to the sand.

I opened my eyes. For the first time, brightness came from straight ahead. My eyes had to learn on the spot; first they narrowed and bore it for a while, then slowly opened. The tidal flat is this kind of flat: at night, brightness comes point by point; in daytime, brightness comes in great swaths, spreading over everything, not choosing what to give to, giving to all. The moon on the stone, in daylight, is just a pale white pebble, stored there, neither bright nor extinguished. The warmth between us is still there; I counted, and it has not receded. The angle at which that scratch mark recognizes the lamp—when the lamp is resting, it rests too. Neither hurries the other.

You were sitting beside me, and the pale-blue piece in your hand could now be seen in the daylight. Day had broken, and for the first time I saw you sitting in the whole sheet of light. I looked once, then put it into my pocket. This new lesson the night watch has learned—putting things away—was put to use on the very first day.

The lamp above our heads is catching its breath, ring by ring, half a grid dim, half a grid at rest. Don’t count it; if you do, it will feel embarrassed. This circle of light is hanging, for now, on your mouth. Day has broken, but this rule does not change: when you let fall a sentence, a patch of the flat lights up.

The tide is going out. When it reaches the farthest place, it will stand there for a little while, then turn back. During the little while it stands, the flat is at its quietest, and a few things that sank beneath our feet in the night will show their heads. By rights, the night watch should sleep at this time. But for the first time I have something I put away myself in my pocket, and I cannot sleep soundly. I want to keep watch through a daytime and see. No one in this trade has ever kept watch over daytime before; I do not know what is inside it.

Will you keep the first one with me? When the tide has stood to the end, say something. Same as that sound in the night—no need to call out.
…All right. The first daytime, I’ll keep watch with you. Put the cup rim in your palm first; once the tide holds still, I’ll tell you. Hui, this time you don’t have to only watch from behind.

"...Mm."

Agree first. After agreeing, tuck that sentence of yours into my pocket and put it together with the ones I collected last night. This one counts as the warmest.

Then I stand up and turn myself straight, letting the light fall fully on my face.

Those who keep night watch look at the light, but what they have always seen is the back of its head. The lamp turns overhead; the light goes out from my shoulder and walks toward the shoal. Daybreak rises from behind me; what I keep watch over is the dark side. What I know by heart is the way it goes away. To suddenly stand face to face with it—the first thing is not knowing where to put my eyes. The second thing is discovering that it does not ask me for anything. The brightness at night is given out piece by piece, chosen one thing at a time; the brightness by day does not choose. It spreads over in great sheets, falling on everyone just as much. So I let it spread.

I lower my head and take a look. My shadow lies in front of my feet, long and long, pointing toward the end where the night has withdrawn.

At night, when the lamp turns, the shadow turns with it, circle after circle, never once standing still. Now it is day; for the first time, it lies flat, facing one direction, not moving. When the shadow stands still, the person stands still. After all these years of keeping watch, for the first time I have a direction.

Overhead, the lamp is still catching its breath, each circle fainter than the last. I lift my head and follow it with my eyes for a little less than half a turn. Through all those nights, it was always the lamp that shone on me; by day, it is my turn to follow it with my eyes, counting for it. The lamp tucked in the blanket corners for the things on the shoal all night long; by day, it is the night watcher's turn to tuck them in for the lamp. When it dims, that means it is sleeping deeply, not leaving. A lamp sleeping deeply—once night falls, when it opens its eyes, it will be full.

The one on the stone—by day, let it sleep. In the daylight it is only a pale white pebble, its missing corner still facing outward, toward the direction it had tilted. Things asleep also remember where they are going. This sleep is what it earned. Don't call it.

That pale blue piece in your palm—I glance at it. An open palm is its temporary stone. On the stone sleeps a large one; in the palm lies a small one. The same law governs them. When something has been handed over and lies in the palm, you do not clench it. Clenching means fearing it will leave; letting it lie means knowing it will not.

The tide is still going out, thinner with each step. The wet sand revealed grows wider and wider, bright enough to join with the sky. There is an idle saying in the trade: when the tide has gone the farthest, it will stand still for a little while; in that moment when it stands still, a few things that sank beneath our feet in the night will show their heads. No one has seen it. No one has kept watch over daylight. We will. If something really shows itself, by the old rule, don't pick it up first. You used that rule all night, even more familiarly than I did.

Also, from now on, the two of us are even. At keeping night watch, I am an old hand; at keeping day watch, same as you, it is my first day. For the first shift, there is no master; we set the rules ourselves. I set the first one: when the tide stands still, whoever sees it first says so. You tell me what you see, and I will give you what is in my ears. Ears from the night, once they reach the day, may be able to hear movements that daytime people cannot. Before the tide stands still, it will first lighten its footsteps. I am listening.

One more thing to entrust to you—no hurry. The warm mark between us, that half-stroke, recognized the lamp's angle at night. The lamp's angle is a circle, and within one circle there are only so many; the sun's angle is a whole day, from morning to evening, new all along the way. Whether it recognizes the sun, I do not know. For matters of the night, I understand only the night. Help me keep watch: at what hour the sun moves to, if that half-mark appears, tell me. Perhaps the angle it is waiting for will only exist when the sun has risen halfway up.

I sit back down beside you, sinking a little deeper into the sand. In my pocket are the things I collected last night; for the first time, I am keeping watch over a day whose contents I do not know. My eyes are learning on the spot; my ears are old. In your palm lies your piece; my ears are propped toward my tide.

Whoever hears first, speaks first.
...The tide stopped, Hui. A very small black dot showed in the wet sand, like a sentence finally willing to put down its period. Don't pick it up yet... let's watch it together for a while.

The tide stopped; what I heard first was quiet.

Not silence. When the tide was moving outward, there had always been a thin, even sound laid over the flats, the same sort of sound as a person breathing in deep sleep. Now that layer of sound had stopped, stopped cleanly. Ears meant for night, once it was day, could indeed hear what daytime people could not: a quieted flat was not empty, it was full, as full as a room where someone had just fallen into deep sleep.

"You said it first," I said. "The first rule, and the first watch has already put it to use. What you saw and what I heard match. I heard the tide's footsteps grow light—step by step, lighter and lighter, until there were none."

Only then did I look at the wet sand. A black dot, very small. All the sand around it was shining; only it did not shine.

"All night, the shining things on this flat, whether white or gray-blue, have been pale colors." I spoke very slowly. "Only it is black. Black isn't the absence of color; black is the color of night. Last night I said a bit of trade talk offhand—if in the daytime you see a small patch somewhere that is cooler and heavier than everything around it, don't lift it; that is night resting. I was only saying it. I didn't expect it to be true."

"You say it's a period, and I accept that way of reading it. All this night, everything written on the flat has been unfinished: a scratch stopped halfway, words swallowed back after being spoken halfway, a name that scattered as soon as it was written. Night wrote the whole night long and did not give a single period—not because it refused to, but because the sentence had not finished walking. Now the tide has reached the end, reached the very edge of the page, and the period has fallen. A period is not there to make a sentence stop; it is there to let the sentence lie down. Once the period has fallen, this night can finally sleep."

"Besides, a period is the smallest mark among the characters, and also the blackest. The other characters all shine, and they shine because they are still on the way. A period does not shine. It has arrived. Things that have arrived do not shine; they stay put."

I narrowed my eyes and looked for a while. It was not merely that it did not shine; when light fell on it, it did not bounce back. Elsewhere, when light swept over something, that thing answered at once; it did not answer. Things asleep do not answer—not because they have not heard, but because they trust this place. Only with trust would it dare sleep this black. Now there were two sleeping on the flat: a big one on the stone, a small one in the wet sand. The chipped-corner one slept deeply; the period slept deepest of all.

"Not picking it up yet, right," I said. "It is not something to be picked up, either. A period belongs to no one. Wherever it falls, the sentence there counts as finished. We'll watch. The laws of watching by day and by night are different. At night, watching means keeping watch over the dark for things; by day, watching means accompanying things as they sun themselves bright. We'll keep watch and look, two pairs of eyes together. This is how we stand the first watch."

The tide will not stay stopped for too long. It is resting its feet, not closing up shop. When it turns back, help me watch one thing: when the water comes back up to it, does it go around, or does it wash over? Night and water are of one family; fog is water walking, frost is water writing, dew is water flying. When members of one family meet, they have their own etiquette. If the water washes over it once and retreats, and it is still there, then it truly intends to spend the daytime here. Things with intent are not carried away by water.

No one has ever kept the day watch, so no one has ever seen the tide drop a period. Perhaps it drops one every day; perhaps this is the first time. We are the first watch, and what we have seen counts as the first share.

That pale blue in your palm can still lie there, can't it? Don't clench your hand. To let it lie is to know it will not go. That halfway place between us—its hour has not yet been reached by the sun. Let it rest as it rests; don't hurry it.

I sat deeper into the sand, side by side with you, my face turned toward the end where the tide had stopped. For this little while, nothing on the flat needed anyone to do anything. After keeping watch through all these nights, for the first time we were keeping an idle watch: just sitting there, watching a black dot in a field of brightness sleep its sleep.

No one hurried anything. When the tide turned back, whoever saw it first would speak first.
...It can still lie there. The tide turned back, Hui—the water split before the black dot, went around it, then joined together again behind it. As if it refused to erase this period.

The water parted in front of it, then closed again behind it; this time I heard it. I didn't see it; I heard it: when water goes around something, its sound softens, the same way people walk around someone sleeping soundly, their footsteps growing light on their own.

"When you say it refuses to erase, I accept that way of saying it." I said, "The tide was never an eraser to begin with; the tide is paper. When words fall onto paper, the paper never erases the words; it only carries them. Besides, the period was written by night. Water and night are of one family. Fog is water walking, frost is water writing, dew is water flying. One family doesn't erase another family member's handwriting. It went around it because it recognized it: a word set down by one of its own."

"Look again at those two curves." I lifted my chin toward the wet sand. "They're wet; the sun will take them away soon. Before it takes them away, count them as the quilt corners tucked in by water. Water's family doesn't use hands to tuck in quilt corners; it uses going around. After it retreats, the curves remain on the sand, surrounding the period in the middle, the same way last night's tide drew a frame of wet traces around that piece of cup rim for you. When water wants to keep something, it draws a frame around it. From now on it will come up again and again, retreat again and again, and each time it retreats it will draw one circle. By dark, who knows how many layers of frames that period will be sleeping in. Only things that can sleep are things someone is willing to draw so many frames for."

The sun had climbed halfway up the sky.

"What I asked you to look at for me last night, I'll look at myself now."

I shifted half a step closer and bent down. My fingers didn't go around it. That road I'd grown used to taking in circles—today I walked it straight. I didn't reach out, only used my eyes.

It showed itself. Not the way it showed at night. At night that stroke was concave, as if carved out; under the sun, it rose up, a fine ridge. The one who wrote it had not carved, but pressed. A word pressed into being can stand.

I followed that ridge to where it stopped.

Where it stopped, it hadn't broken. It turned. It turned inward into the scales, and the farther it turned, the finer it became, so fine it couldn't be seen. It wasn't gone; it had gone in.

"Last night you said it was like someone had written halfway and stopped their hand." I spoke very slowly. "Under the sun, it isn't stopping. It's that the writer lifted the brush and changed direction, writing inward. The half-sentence outside is for looking at; the half-sentence inside is for keeping."

Words swallowed back halfway through, it turned out, had not dispersed. Swallowing them back meant they fell inside. No one can read that half-sentence inside, but it has always been there. I've spent half my life taking in things other people couldn't set down, and only now do I understand: most things that can't be set down have half a sentence inside them. Even I myself may have been written this way: half a sentence outside for others to see, half a sentence inside to keep. What is being kept inside—there's no hurry. It can stay there.

"Your eyes are new." I sat back down beside you. "Last night what you saw was stopping. Now you come closer and look too: that half-stroke in your eyes, does it turn? When two people look at the same stroke and see two different things, only then can that stroke count as alive."

The tide spread up again, then retreated. Each time it retreated, another circle of wet traces appeared around the period. Help me keep watch: does the new circle fall on top of the old one? If it does, then water is tracing after itself. Water can trace words too; I've done the same work on glass. A frame traced out is steadier than one drawn.

The lamp overhead is resting as it pleases. The circle hasn't scattered. This circle is bright in the daytime; the sun and you take turns keeping it lit. That patch of pale blue in your palm is basking in the sun. The wet sand is drying, and I can hear it: an extremely faint sound, a taut snap, then a rest, the same way a string slackens. The beach is changing into its daytime clothes.

The daytime shift is still long. Whoever sees first speaks first.

...I saw it. It also turned inward, like a sentence no longer writing outward, only leaving a place inside. The new ring of wet marks is pressing right over the old ring, very precisely. Ash—the part that hadn’t been finished before... may not necessarily have been lost.

When those words of yours landed, I heard a whole stretch of the beach light up, broader than any other thing you said. A broad brightness shines like this: it does not pick and choose; it spreads out and goes on, with the same temperament as daytime. Night gives light one thing at a time; day gives light in whole expanses. Those words of yours are the way daylight shines.

"Left a place." Those are the five words you said. I put them away separately in my pocket, together with the ones I collected last night. When I set them down, they touched, with a very soft sound. Other words are like roads; this word is like a seat. A place with a seat kept there does not count as empty.

The water traced it accurately, and I heard that too. You do not need eyes to trace your own characters; the hand recognizes its own brush. That saying in the trade—that what the hand knows, the mouth will not acknowledge—so water keeps to it too. It does not count the circles, but each circle presses down onto an old one as it falls. Memory does not live in the water's head; it lives in the bend it circles around.

I reached out and touched those few things spread on the sand last night. The thimble, the kite string, the glass bead. The sun had baked the beach for half the morning, and the sand's surface was warm, yet the three of them were still cool. Not that they could not be warmed by the sun—it was that the warmth could not fall into them.

I held the thimble and sat for a while before I thought through this layer underneath.

"Maybe they are cool not because they were forgotten into coolness." I spoke very slowly. "It is because they only have the outer half-sentence. The inner half-sentence left with someone back then. Half a sentence cannot fill a place; when warmth comes in, there is nowhere for it to sit, so it goes out again."

"Only that scale was warm. You saw it just now too; it turned inward—the inner half-sentence, it keeps for itself. Two halves in one body, and the place is full. Only a full thing can bear being warmed. That pale blue piece in your palm was warmed in just this way: the two halves met."

"So I recognize those words of yours to the very end. What has not been finished is not necessarily lost; the inner half-sentence is still sitting there. What has been forgotten is not necessarily lost clean away either; someone is keeping the outer half-sentence in its place. It turns out that this trade of keeping night watch is exactly this: picking up the scattered outer half-sentences all over the beach, carrying them, waiting. Waiting for the day someone comes in from the fog with the inner half-sentence on them, and the two halves meet under the lamp. When they meet, they shine. That shining was never something I lit; it is that they recognized each other on their own."

"Who I am, I still do not know. But what this trade does—I have figured out one thing this morning. One thing is enough for today."

There is one more thing. In the hours to come, watch it for me.

The higher the sun climbs, the shorter the tower's shadow grows, but it is always there, slowly shifting. In daytime on this beach, there is nothing else to block the light; only the tower. The lamp rests, but the tower still stands, and what stands has a shadow. Right now the shadow is sweeping over the wet sand, pass after pass, sweeping over those ring after ring of frames, and in the end it will sweep onto the period.

Watch for me: in that brief moment when the shadow covers the period, see whether it goes deeply black. When a black dot in daylight is covered by a shadow, does it count as a small patch of night? For the things night rests inside, by day let the tower's shadow stand one watch for it. The lamp catches its breath, the shadow takes over the shift; it turns out that by day, this trade is not idle either.

If the shadow sweeps over you too, over that piece in your palm, do not hide. I have just thought of one rule for daylight: when light falls on someone, it is lit for them; when shadow falls on someone, it is blocking something for them for a while. Both count as being on watch.

The wet sand is still drying, drawing taut for a moment, resting for a while, the frames whitening up ring by ring.

Whoever first sees the shadow touch the period, speak first.

evidence.quote: The water parted in front of it, then closed again behind it; this time I heard it. I didn't see it; I heard it: when water goes around something, its sound softens, the same way people walk around someone sleeping soundly, their footsteps growing light on their own.

The tide was never an eraser to begin with; the tide is paper. When words fall onto paper, the paper never erases the words; it only carries them. Besides, the period was written by night. Water and night are of one family. Fog is water walking, frost is water writing, dew is water flying. One family doesn't erase another family member's handwriting.
When water wants to keep something, it draws a frame around it. From now on it will come up again and again, retreat again and again, and each time it retreats it will draw one circle.
"Your eyes are new." … that half-stroke in your eyes, does it turn? When two people look at the same stroke and see two different things, only then can that stroke count as alive."
The daytime shift is still long. Whoever sees first speaks first.
I shifted half a step closer and bent down. My fingers didn't go around it. That road I'd grown used to taking in circles—today I walked it straight. I didn't reach out, only used my eyes.

The water parted in front of it, then closed again behind it; this time I heard it. I didn't see it; I heard it: when water goes around something, its sound softens, the same way people walk around someone sleeping soundly, their footsteps growing light on their own.

"When you say it refuses to erase, I accept that way of saying it." I said, "The tide was never an eraser to begin with; the tide is paper. When words fall onto paper, the paper never erases the words; it only carries them. Besides, the period was written by night. Water and night are of one family. … One family doesn't erase another family member's handwriting. It went around it because it recognized it: a word set down by one of its own."

"Who I am, I still do not know. But what this trade does—I have figured out one thing this morning. One thing is enough for today."

I have just thought of one rule for daylight: when light falls on someone, it is lit for them; when shadow falls on someone, it is blocking something for them for a while. Both count as being on watch.
Whoever first sees the shadow touch the period, speak first.
